arXiv:2604.24337v3 [quant-ph] 03 Aug 2026

New non-Euclidean neural quantum states from hyperbolic Lorentz recurrent architectures

H. L. Dao Note: espoirdujour1162@gmail.com
August 24, 2026
Abstract

In this work, we construct new non-Euclidean neural quantum states (NQS) based on hyperbolic Lorentz recurrent architectures (RNN/GRU). These constructions, together with the Poincaré RNN NQS also newly constructed here, extend the class of previously introduced non-Eucllidean NQS which consists only of Poincaré hyperbolic GRU. Using the Heisenberg J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} and J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} models consisting of 100 spins in the Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) setting, we show that the four hyperbolic RNN/GRU NQS variants are always able to furnish better representations of the ground state wavefunctions of the quantum systems than their respective Euclidean counterparts with the same architecture. In our experiments, among the four hyperbolic NQS, Lorentz RNN stands out in particular because despite having almost three times fewer parameters, it is capable of surpassing the more complex Poincaré GRU and Lorentz GRU to emerge as the best overall hyperbolic NQS ansatz on many instances involving different J2J_{2} and (J2,J3J_{2},J_{3}) couplings. Given the findings from this work showing that the four newly constructed hyperbolic RNN/GRU NQS ansätze are able to outperform the well-established Euclidean RNN/GRU NQS in Heisenberg spin models, we establish the utility and efficiency of the hyperbolic Lorentz RNN/GRU NQS as well as the Poincaré RNN/GRU NQS for future variational studies of quantum many-body systems, especially those exhibiting a hierarchical structure in the form of the different degrees of nearest-neighbor interactions.

1 Introduction

The field of neural quantum states (NQS) that utilizes neural networks to approximate ground state wavefunctions of quantum many-body systems, most notably spin systems such as the Transverse Field Ising Model (TFIM) and Heisenberg J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} models, have been expanding rapidly since the introduction of the Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) as the first type of NQS in the seminal works [1], [2]. Since then, many different types of NQS based on different neural network architectures such as simple artificial neural networks (ANN) ([3], [4]), convolutional neural networks (CNNs) ([5], [6], [7]), recurrent neural networks (RNNs) ([11], [12], [13], [14]), and transformers ([15], [16], [17], [18], [19]) - to name a few - have been developed in rapid succession. While these works explored the various advantages that the many different neural network architectures had to offer and showed that they could deliver impressive results, the one single constant among them all is the fact that they are all conventional Euclidean constructions. In other words, the mathematical operations underlying their constructions are defined on Euclidean space. It was not until [22] that the first type of non-Euclidean NQS ansatz was introduced in the form of the Poincaré hyperbolic GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit [24] - a specialized form of RNNs), whose underlying construction made use of the geometry of the Poincaré disk model of hyperbolic space, based on the prior work [8] in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) that first introduced the hyperbolic Poincaré RNN/GRU networks for the NLP tasks of sentence embeddings, textual entailment and noisy-prefix recognition. In NLP, later works on hyperbolic neural networks [27]-[33] have consistently shown that they are capable of outperforming their Euclidean counterparts, especially when the involved datasets have hierarchical, tree-like structures. This has to do with the fact that hyperbolic space can embed tree-like structures with very low distortions [10], thanks to the property that hyperbolic geometry allows for an exponential expansion of space (area or volume) as a function of the radial distance, unlike Euclidean space, which grows only polynomially with distance [35], [36], [37].

As a proof of concept, in [22], it was shown that the then-newly introduced hyperbolic NQS ansatz based on Poincaré GRU (referred to simply as ‘hyperbolic GRU’ in [22]) could definitively outperform the ordinary NQS ansätze based on Euclidean GRU and RNN in the three settings of the two-dimensional TFIM of up to 81 spins, the one-dimensional Heisenberg J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model with 50 spins, and the one-dimensional Heisenberg J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model with 30 spins. In particular, the outperformance delivered by Poincaré GRU was definitive when the systems under consideration exhibited a clear hierarchical structures, such as the three cases mentioned above which involved different competing degrees of nearest neighbor interactions. It was hypothesized in [22] that an NQS ansatz based on hyperbolic GRU would likely outperform one based on Euclidean GRU in all such quantum many-body systems, including those already considered but with much larger system sizes. Furthermore, the work [22] also hypothesized the possibility of potentially similar outperformances delivered by other types of hyperbolic NQS ansätze over their Euclidean versions. While these yet-to-be-constructed hyperbolic NQS ansätze could be based on any kind of different architectures, such as CNNs, RBMs or transformers, the most immediate and natural extension of [22] would arguably be the construction of the hyperbolic version of the simpler RNN architecture, which was not done in [22], as well as the construction of both the RNN and GRU architectures using the Lorentz model of hyperbolic space, which is believed to have the potential to outperform the Poincaré hyperbolic model with the same architecture.

In this work, our main motivations and results are summarized below.

  • •

    As a first step, we constructed and introduced three new types of hyperbolic RNN NQS ansätze: Poincaré RNN, Lorentz RNN and Lorentz GRU, alongside the Poincaré GRU11 1 The four variants will be collectively referred to as hyperbolic RNNs. originally introduced in our previous work [22]. Incidentally, to the best of our knowledge, the Lorentz RNN and Lorentz GRU in this work are the first standalone constructions of their kinds in the literature, i.e. the first constructions where RNN/GRU architectures are used in conjunction with the Lorentz geometry. In the NLP literature where hyperbolic neural networks originated, only the Poincaré GRU/RNN were explicitly formulated in the works of [8], and while many different neural network architectures based on Lorentz geometry incorporating some forms of recurrent gates were explored in later NLP works (such as [9]), none explicitly constructed the Lorentz RNN or Lorentz GRU as standalone, independent architectures. More specifically, while Lorentz embeddings [44], Lorentz feed-forward layers, and Lorentz attention [27] were widely used as a direct result of the transition from Poincaré geometry to Lorentz geometry in the NLP context, a standalone Lorentz RNN/GRU gating mechanism was never formally formulated. The recurrent gating equations operating natively on the Lorentz hyperboloid are only explicitly derived and benchmarked in this work in the context of many-body quantum physics.

  • •

    Secondly, using the settings of the one-dimensional Heisenberg J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} and J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} models with 100 spins, which is two times larger than the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model and three times larger than the J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model considered in [22], we carried out the variational Monte-Carlo (VMC) experiments using six types of NQS ansätze: Euclidean RNN/GRU, Poincaré RNN/GRU, Lorentz RNN/GRU to benchmark the performances of all four hyperbolic RNNs against their Euclidean counterparts. As first raised in [22], the primary question to settle in this work is still whether, in the specific larger-size Heisenberg quantum many-body systems under study, these collective hyperbolic RNN NQS can outperform the Euclidean NQS with the same architecture. However, with the inclusion of the new types of hyperbolic RNNs, additional questions also arise regarding the performances of different NQS ansätze constructed from different models or representations of hyperbolic space relative to each other. More specifically, the secondary question to explore in this work is, which hyperbolic sub-model, Lorentz or Poincaré, will definitively proves to be better.

    While the primary question regarding the outperformance of the collective hyperbolic RNN NQS over the Euclidean NQS can be affirmatively confirmed, the secondary question is less definitively so, since a different hyperbolic model emerged as the top performing NQS in a different coupling regime of the Heisenberg mdel under study. This perhaps has less to do with the efficiency or effectiveness of the NQS models themselves than with the physics of the problem, more specifically, it makes sense that with different underlying physics (represented by the small or large coupling constants J2J_{2} and (J2,J3)(J_{2},J_{3}) in the system), no single hyperbolic NQS ansatz can always emerge as the best approximation to the true ground state every single time. Instead, what we would see from the results of this work is that on the majority of the occasions, out of the four new hyperbolic RNN variants, Lorentz RNN emerged as the top performing variant, surpassing both Poincaré GRU and Lorentz GRU, while on another occasion, Poincaré GRU was the top performer, and on the remaining occasion, Lorentz GRU took the top spot. The emergence of the Lorentz RNN as the overall best hyperbolic NQS variant, despite having three times fewer parameters than Lorentz/Poincaré GRU (and Euclidean GRU), shows that it is a parameter-efficient construction that is valuable to future VMC studies of all kinds of quantum many-body systems beyond spin models.

This paper is orgarnized as follows: In Section 2, we detail the mathematical constructions of the Poincaré RNN and GRU (Section 2.1), as well as the constructions of the Lorentz RNN and GRU (Section 2.2). In Section 3, we use these newly constructed hyperbolic RNNs to build new non-Euclidean, hyperbolic NQS ansätze. In Section 4 and 5, we report and discuss the results of the VMC experiments using the six types of (hyperbolic and Euclidean) NQS ansätze in the Heisenberg J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} and Heisenberg J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model, respectively. In Section 6, we summarize the findings of this work and describe some possible future directions. In the Appendix, Section 7.1 discusses the effects of spatial constraint hyperparameters on the performances of the Lorentz and Poincaré hyperbolic neural networks, Sections 7.2.1 and 7.2.2 include the full results of all NQS ansätze from different VMC runs using different random seeds.

The Python codes used in this work to construct the hyperbolic Poincaré RNN/GRU NQS are the Pytorch translation of the TensorFlow codes22 2 which can be found at the Github directory: https://github.com/lorrespz/nqs_hyperbolic_rnn written for our earlier work [22], while the codes used to construct the Lorentz RNN/GRU NQS are built from the Poincaré version, but the actual construction of the Lorentz RNN/GRU hyperbolic networks, which formed the main component of the Lorentz-based NQS ansätze, are based on the hypercore library [20] with some modifications. In particular, we used the files lmath.py and lorentzian.py from the subdirectory manifolds of the main directory hypercore_main to construct the Lorentz RNN and Lorentz GRU33 3 The library hypercore offers a comprehensive toolbox for Lorentz-based hyperbolic models, and comes with many full-fledged hyperbolic networks that are preconstructed by the authors such as Lorentz MLP, Lorentz CNN, Lorentz Graph Neural Network, and Lorentz transformers. However, the RNN-based family of models containing RNN, GRU and LSTM (Long Short Term Memory) are not among these preconstructed models. The Lorentz RNN and GRU are constructed for this first time as independend, standalone architectures in this work. . All Python codes and trained neural networks for this work can be found at this Github repository: https://github.com/lorrespz/hypnqs_lorentz_poincare.

2 Two variants of hyperbolic RNNs

The constructions of the Poincaré and Lorentz variants of hyperbolic RNNs are based on the following definitions of Euclidean RNN and GRU. Starting with an input vector x→i∈ℝdx\vec{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} at step ii of size dxd_{x}, the conventional version of RNN is a function that relates the hidden state vector h→i∈ℝdh\vec{h}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} of size dhd_{h} to the input x→i\vec{x}_{i} and the same hidden state vector h→i−1\vec{h}_{i-1} at the previous time step (i−1)(i-1)

RNN:\displaystyle\text{RNN}: h→i=f⁡(Wh​h→i−1+Uh​x→i+b→h),\displaystyle\vec{h}_{i}=f(W_{h}\vec{h}_{i-1}+U_{h}\vec{x}_{i}+\vec{b}_{h})\,, (1)

where ff is a nonlinear activation function (often ‘tanh’), WhW_{h} is a dh×dhd_{h}\times d_{h} weight matrix, UhU_{h} is a dh×dxd_{h}\times d_{x} weight matrix, and bh∈ℝdhb_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} is a vector of size dhd_{h} known as the bias.

GRU [24] is a more sophisticated version of RNN with additional structures comprising the reset gate r→i∈ℝdh\vec{r}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} and the update gate z→i∈ℝdh\vec{z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}. The defining equations of the conventional or Euclidean GRU are

GRU:\displaystyle\text{GRU}: r→i=σ⁡(Wr​h→i−1+Ur​x→i+b→r)\displaystyle\vec{r}_{i}={\sigma}\left(W_{r}\vec{h}_{i-1}+U_{r}\vec{x}_{i}+\vec{b}_{r}\right) (2)
z→i=σ⁡(Wz​h→i−1+Uz​x→i+b→z)\displaystyle\vec{z}_{i}={\sigma}\left(W_{z}\vec{h}_{i-1}+U_{z}\vec{x}_{i}+\vec{b}_{z}\right)
h~→i=f⁡[Wh​(r→i⊙h→i−1)+Uh​x→i+b→h]\displaystyle\vec{\tilde{h}}_{i}=f\left[W_{h}(\vec{r}_{i}\odot\vec{h}_{i-1})+U_{h}\vec{x}_{i}+\vec{b}_{h}\right]
h→i=(1−z→i)⊙h→i−1+z→i⊙h~→i\displaystyle\vec{h}_{i}=(1-\vec{z}_{i})\odot\vec{h}_{i-1}+\vec{z}_{i}\odot\vec{\tilde{h}}_{i}

In Eq.(2), h→i\vec{h}_{i} is the final hidden state at step ii while h~→i\vec{\tilde{h}}_{i} is the new state computed in the same time step, ff is a nonlinear activation function (often taken to be ‘tanh’), σ{\sigma} is the sigmoid activation, x→i\vec{x}_{i} is the input vector of length dxd_{x}, Wh,Wz,WrW_{h},W_{z},W_{r} are the dh×dhd_{h}\times d_{h} weight matrices, Uh,Uz,UrU_{h},U_{z},U_{r} are the dh×dxd_{h}\times d_{x} weight matrices, b→h,b→z,b→r∈ℝdh\vec{b}_{h},\vec{b}_{z},\vec{b}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} are the bias vectors, and ⊙\odot is the pointwise multiplication operation. Note that for GRU, the last equation appearing in Eq.(2) that defines the final hidden state h→i\vec{h}_{i} can also be written as follows

h→i=h→i−1+z→i⊙(−h→i−1+h~→i),\displaystyle\vec{h}_{i}=\vec{h}_{i-1}+\vec{z}_{i}\odot(-\vec{h}_{i-1}+\vec{\tilde{h}}_{i})\,, (3)

where the update step involves the previous state h→i−1\vec{h}_{i-1} and the new state h~→i\vec{\tilde{h}}_{i}, which is a function of the reset gate r→i\vec{r}_{i}, the previous state h→i−1\vec{h}_{i-1} and the input x→i\vec{x}_{i}. When z→i≈0\vec{z}_{i}\approx 0, the final state h→i\vec{h}_{i} is almost entirely h~→i\vec{\tilde{h}}_{i} - the new state. When z→i≈1\vec{z}_{i}\approx 1, the final state h→i\vec{h}_{i} is almost entirely its previous state h→i−1\vec{h}_{i-1}. When r→i≈1\vec{r}_{i}\approx 1 and z→i≈1\vec{z}_{i}\approx 1, the GRU essentially reduces to the RNN [25].

2.1 Construction of Poincare hyperbolic RNN/GRU

The Poincaré ball model (𝔻N,g𝔻)(\mathbb{D}^{N},g^{\mathbb{D}}) of hyperbolic space is defined by the manifold 𝔻N\mathbb{D}^{N}

𝔻cN={x∈ℝN:c​‖x‖<1}\displaystyle\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}:c||x||<1\right\} (4)

where the parameter cc is the Poincaré ball’s radius. When c=0c=0, 𝔻cN=ℝN\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c}=\mathbb{R}^{N}, while when c>0c>0, 𝔻cN\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c} is the open ball of radius 1/c1/\sqrt{c}. In all the computations used in this work, we set c=1c=1. The space 𝔻cN\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c} in Eq.(4) is equipped with the metric

gx𝔻=λx2​gE,λx=21−‖x‖2\displaystyle g^{\mathbb{D}}_{x}=\lambda^{2}_{x}g^{E},\hskip 14.22636pt\lambda_{x}=\frac{2}{1-||x||^{2}} (5)

where gE=𝟏Ng^{E}=\mathbf{1}_{N} is the identity matrix representing the Euclidean metric. The parallel transport P𝟎→xc​(v)P^{c}_{\mathbf{0}\rightarrow x}(v) of a vector v∈T𝟎​𝔻cNv\in T_{\mathbf{0}}\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c} to another tangent space Tx​𝔻cNT_{x}\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c} are defined as

P𝟎→xc(v)=logxc[x⊕cexp𝟎c(v)]\displaystyle P^{c}_{\mathbf{0}\rightarrow x}(v)=\log_{x}^{c}\left[x\oplus_{c}\exp_{\mathbf{0}}^{c}(v)\right] (6)

where the operations log\log and exp\exp are the exponential and logarithmic maps. For any point x∈𝔻cNx\in\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c}, any vector v≠𝟎v\neq\mathbf{0} and any point y≠xy\neq x, the exponential and logarithmic maps expxc:Tx​𝔻cM→𝔻cM\exp^{c}_{x}:T_{x}\mathbb{D}^{M}_{c}\rightarrow\mathbb{D}^{M}_{c} and logxc:𝔻cN→Tx​𝔻cN\log^{c}_{x}:\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c}\rightarrow T_{x}\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c} between the hyperbolic space and its Euclidean tangent space are defined as

expxc⁡(v)\displaystyle\exp_{x}^{c}(v) =\displaystyle= x⊕c[tanh(cλxc​‖v‖2)vc​‖v‖]\displaystyle x\oplus_{c}\left[\tanh\left(\sqrt{c}\frac{\lambda_{x}^{c}||v||}{2}\right)\frac{v}{\sqrt{c}||v||}\right] (7)
logxc⁡(y)\displaystyle\log_{x}^{c}(y) =\displaystyle= 2c​λxctanh−1(c||−x⊕cy||)−x⊕cy||−x⊕cy||\displaystyle\frac{2}{\sqrt{c}{\lambda}_{x}^{c}}\tanh^{-1}\left(\sqrt{c}||-x\oplus_{c}y||\right)\frac{-x\oplus_{c}y}{||-x\oplus_{c}y||} (8)

where λxc=2/(1−c​‖x‖2){\lambda}_{x}^{c}=2/(1-c||x||^{2}). When x=𝟎x=\mathbf{0}, the above maps take more compact forms

exp𝟎c⁡(v)\displaystyle\exp_{\mathbf{0}}^{c}(v) =\displaystyle= tanh⁡(c​‖v‖)​vc​‖v‖(T𝟎M​𝔻cM→𝔻cM)\displaystyle\tanh\left(\sqrt{c}||v||\right)\frac{v}{\sqrt{c}||v||}\,\,\qquad\left(T_{\mathbf{0}_{M}}\mathbb{D}^{M}_{c}\rightarrow\mathbb{D}^{M}_{c}\right) (9)
log𝟎c⁡(y)\displaystyle\log_{\mathbf{0}}^{c}(y) =\displaystyle= tanh−1⁡(c​‖y‖)​yc​‖y‖(𝔻cN→T𝟎N​𝔻cN).\displaystyle\tanh^{-1}\left(\sqrt{c}||y||\right)\frac{y}{\sqrt{c}||y||}\qquad\left(\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c}\rightarrow T_{\mathbf{0}_{N}}\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c}\right)\,. (10)

Poincaré hyperbolic RNNs were discussed in detail in [22] but for the sake of completeness, we will summarize their constructions here. The Poincaré hyperbolic RNN and hyperbolic GRU are defined by the following formulae

Hyperbolic RNN:\displaystyle\text{Hyperbolic RNN}: h→i=(Wh⊗ch→i−1)⊕c(Uh⊗cx→i)⊕cb→h\displaystyle\vec{h}_{i}=(W_{h}\otimes_{c}\vec{h}_{i-1})\oplus_{c}(U_{h}\otimes_{c}\vec{x}_{i})\oplus_{c}\frac{}{}\vec{b}_{h} (11)
Hyperbolic GRU:\displaystyle\text{Hyperbolic GRU}: r→i=σ{log𝟎c[(Wr⊗ch→i−1)⊕c(Ur⊗cx→i)⊕cb→r]},\displaystyle\vec{r}_{i}={\sigma}\,\left\{\log_{\mathbf{0}}^{c}\left[(W_{r}\otimes_{c}\vec{h}_{i-1})\oplus_{c}(U_{r}\otimes_{c}\vec{x}_{i})\oplus_{c}\frac{}{}\vec{b}_{r}\right]\right\}\,, (12)
z→i=σ{log𝟎c[(Wz⊗ch→i−1)⊕c(Uz⊗cx→i)⊕cb→z]},\displaystyle\vec{z}_{i}={\sigma}\,\left\{\log_{\mathbf{0}}^{c}\left[(W_{z}\otimes_{c}\vec{h}_{i-1})\oplus_{c}(U_{z}\otimes_{c}\vec{x}_{i})\oplus_{c}\frac{}{}\vec{b}_{z}\right]\right\}\,,
h~→i=Wh⊗c(r→i⊙ch→i−1)⊕c(Uh⊗cx→i)⊕cb→h,\displaystyle\vec{\tilde{h}}_{i}=W_{h}\,\otimes_{c}(\vec{r}_{i}\odot_{c}\vec{h}_{i-1})\oplus_{c}(U_{h}\otimes_{c}\vec{x}_{i})\frac{}{}\oplus_{c}\vec{b}_{h}\,,
h→i=h→i−1⊕cz→i⊙c(−h→i−1⊕ch~→i).\displaystyle\vec{h}_{i}=\vec{h}_{i-1}\oplus_{c}\,\vec{z}_{i}\,\odot_{c}\left(-\vec{h}_{i-1}\oplus_{c}\vec{\tilde{h}}_{i}\right)\,.

In Eqs.(11), (12), the various weight matrices Wh,r,zW_{h,r,z} and Uh,r,zU_{h,r,z} have the same meanings as in the Euclidean RNN/GRU case - Eqs.(1), (2), but the hidden state vector h→i∈𝔻cdh\vec{h}_{i}\in\mathbb{D}^{d_{h}}_{c}, input vector x→i∈𝔻cdi\vec{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{D}^{d_{i}}_{c}, and bias vectors b→h,r,z∈𝔻cdh\vec{b}_{h,r,z}\in\mathbb{D}^{d_{h}}_{c} are all vectors on the Poincaré disk. The nonlinear activation function ff (often tanh) used in the Euclidean RNN/GRU is not used in the hyperbolic case (in this work) because hyperbolic space itself provides some degree of nonlinearity. The mathematical operations ⊕c,⊗c,⊙c\oplus_{c},\otimes_{c},\odot_{c} appearing in the equations above are the Poincaré hyperbolic analogs of the Euclidean addition, matrix multiplication and pointwise multiplication. Although these formulae were derived in [8] and described in more detail in [22], they are recalled below for the sake of completeness.

  • •

    For x,y∈𝔻cNx,y\in\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c}, the Mobius addition ⊕c\oplus_{c} is

    x⊕cy≡(1+2​c​⟨x,y⟩+c​‖y‖2)​x+(1−c​‖x‖2)​y1+2​c​⟨x,y⟩+c2​‖x‖2​‖y‖2.\displaystyle x\oplus_{c}y\equiv\frac{(1+2c\langle x,y\rangle+c||y||^{2})x+(1-c||x||^{2})y}{1+2c\langle x,y\rangle+c^{2}||x||^{2}||y||^{2}}\,. (13)
  • •

    For x∈𝔻cN\{𝟎}x\in\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c}\backslash\{\mathbf{0}\} and W:ℝM→ℝNW:\mathbb{R}^{M}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{N}, the Mobius matrix multiplication is defined by

    W⊗cx=1c​tanh⁡(‖W​x‖‖x‖​tanh−1⁡(c​‖x‖))​W​x‖W​x‖\displaystyle W\otimes_{c}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{c}}\tanh\left(\frac{||Wx||}{||x||}\tanh^{-1}(\sqrt{c}||x||)\right)\frac{Wx}{||Wx||} (14)
  • •

    For x∈𝔻cN\{𝟎}x\in\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c}\backslash\{\mathbf{0}\} and r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}, the Mobius pointwise multiplication ⊙c\odot_{c}, is defined as

    r⊙cx=1c​tanh⁡(‖r​x‖‖x‖​tanh−1⁡(c​‖x‖))​r​x‖r​x‖\displaystyle r\odot_{c}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{c}}\tanh\left(\frac{||rx||}{||x||}\tanh^{-1}(\sqrt{c}||x||)\right)\frac{rx}{||rx||} (15)

In terms of parallel transport, the Mobius addition for x∈𝔻cNx\in\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c} with b∈𝔻cNb\in\mathbb{D}^{N}_{c} can be written as

x⊕cb=expxc[P𝟎→xc(log𝟎c(b))].\displaystyle x\oplus_{c}b=\exp_{x}^{c}\left[P_{\mathbf{0}\rightarrow x}^{c}\left(\log_{\mathbf{0}}^{c}(b)\frac{}{}\right)\right]\,. (16)

2.2 Construction of Lorentz hyperbolic RNN/GRU

The nn-dimensional Lorentz hyperboloid ℍn\mathbb{H}^{n} with constant negative curvature −k-k where k=1k=1 is given as

ℍn≡{𝐱∈ℝn+1:⟨𝐱,𝐱⟩ℒ=−1,x0>0}\displaystyle\mathbb{H}^{n}\equiv\left\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}=-1,\,x_{0}>0\right\} (17)

where ⟨𝐱,𝐲⟩ℒ\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}, the Lorentzian scalar product for (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional vectors 𝐱,𝐲∈ℝn+1\mathbf{x,y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, is defined as

⟨𝐱,𝐲⟩ℒ≡−x0​y0+∑i=1nxi​yi.\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}\equiv-x_{0}y_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}\,. (18)

Unlike the Poincaré disk where the origin 𝟎P=(0,0,…,0)\mathbf{0}_{P}=(0,0,\ldots,0), in the Lorentz model of hyperbolic space, the origin is the point 𝟎ℒ=(1,0,0,…,0)\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}=(1,0,0,\ldots,0). The distance function between two points 𝐱,𝐲∈ℍn\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{H}^{n} is

dℍ​(𝐱,𝐲)=arcosh​(−⟨𝐱,𝐲⟩ℒ),\displaystyle d_{\mathbb{H}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\text{arcosh}\left(-\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}\right)\,, (19)

while the Lorentzian norm of a vector 𝐯\mathbf{v} is

‖𝐯‖ℒ=⟨𝐯,𝐯⟩ℒ.\displaystyle||\mathbf{v}||_{\mathcal{L}}=\sqrt{\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{v}\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}}\,. (20)

The tangent space at 𝐱\mathbf{x} is the nn-dimensional Euclidean vector space approximating ℍn\mathbb{H}^{n} around 𝐱\mathbf{x}:

𝒯x​ℍn≡{𝐱∈ℝn+1:⟨𝐯,𝐱⟩ℒ=0}\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{x}\mathbb{H}^{n}\equiv\left\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{x}\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}=0\right\} (21)

Similar to the Poincaré model described in the previous section, mappings between the Lorentz hyperboloid and its tangent space are done using the exponential exp𝐱⁡(𝐯)\exp_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{v}) and logarithmic log𝐱⁡(𝐲)\log_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y}) maps.

𝒯𝐱​ℍn→ℍn:\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{x}}\mathbb{H}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{H}^{n}: exp𝐱⁡(𝐯)=cosh⁡(‖𝐯‖ℒ)​𝐱+sinh⁡(‖𝐯‖ℒ)​𝐯‖𝐯‖ℒ\displaystyle\exp_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{v})=\cosh\left(||\mathbf{v}||_{\mathcal{L}}\right)\mathbf{x}+\sinh\left(||\mathbf{v}||_{\mathcal{L}}\right)\frac{\mathbf{v}}{||\mathbf{v}||_{\mathcal{L}}} (22)
ℍn→𝒯𝐱​ℍn:\displaystyle\mathbb{H}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{x}}\mathbb{H}^{n}: log𝐱⁡(𝐲)=dℍ​(𝐱,𝐲)​𝐲+⟨𝐱,𝐲⟩ℒ​𝐱||𝐲+⟨𝐱,𝐲⟩ℒ𝐱||ℒ\displaystyle\log_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{y})=d_{\mathbb{H}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\frac{\mathbf{y}+\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}\,\mathbf{x}}{\left||\mathbf{y}+\langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}\,\mathbf{x}\right||_{\mathcal{L}}} (23)

The parallel transport operation that maps a point 𝐳∈𝒯𝐱​ℍn\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{x}}\mathbb{H}^{n} to a point in 𝒯𝐲​ℍn\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{y}}\mathbb{H}^{n} is defined as

P𝐱→𝐲​(𝐳)=𝐳+⟨𝐲,𝐳⟩ℒ1−⟨(𝐱,𝐲)⟩ℒ​(𝐱+𝐲)\displaystyle P_{\mathbf{x}\rightarrow\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{z}+\frac{\langle\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z}\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}}{1-\langle(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}) (24)

When 𝐱=𝟎ℒ\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}},

P𝟎ℒ→𝐲​(𝐳)=𝐳+⟨𝐲,𝐳⟩ℒ1−⟨(𝟎ℒ,𝐲)⟩ℒ​(𝟎ℒ+𝐲)\displaystyle P_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\mathbf{y}}(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{z}+\frac{\langle\mathbf{y},\mathbf{z}\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}}{1-\langle(\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}},\mathbf{y})\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}}(\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}+\mathbf{y}) (25)

Using the Euclidean definitions of RNN and GRU in Eqs.(1), (2), the Lorentz version of hyperbolic RNN and GRU (referred to as Lorentz RNN and Lorentz GRU, respectively) are defined as

Lorentz RNN:\displaystyle\text{Lorentz RNN}: h→i=(Wh⊗ℒh→i−1)⊕ℒ(Uh⊗ℒx→i)⊕ℒb→h\displaystyle\vec{h}_{i}=\left(W_{h}\otimes_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{h}_{i-1}\right)\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}\left(U_{h}\otimes_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{x}_{i}\right)\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{b}_{h} (26)
Lorentz GRU:\displaystyle\text{Lorentz GRU}: r→i=σ{log𝟎ℒ[(Wr⊗ℒh→i−1)⊕ℒ(Ur⊗ℒx→i)⊕ℒb→r]}\displaystyle\vec{r}_{i}={\sigma}\left\{\log_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}}\left[\left(W_{r}\otimes_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{h}_{i-1}\right)\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}\left(U_{r}\otimes_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{x}_{i}\right)\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{b}_{r}\right]\right\} (27)
z→i=σ{log𝟎ℒ[(Wz⊗ℒh→i−1)⊕ℒ(Uz⊗ℒx→i)⊕ℒb→z]}\displaystyle\vec{z}_{i}={\sigma}\left\{\log_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}}\left[\left(W_{z}\otimes_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{h}_{i-1}\right)\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}\left(U_{z}\otimes_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{x}_{i}\right)\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{b}_{z}\right]\right\}
h~→i=Wh⊗ℒ(r→i⊙ℒh→i−1)⊕ℒ(Uh⊗ℒx→i)⊕ℒb→h,\displaystyle\vec{\tilde{h}}_{i}=W_{h}\,\otimes_{\mathcal{L}}(\vec{r}_{i}\odot_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{h}_{i-1})\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}(U_{h}\otimes_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{x}_{i})\frac{}{}\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{b}_{h}\,,
h→i=h→i−1⊕ℒz→i⊙ℒ(−h→i−1⊕ℒh~→i).\displaystyle\vec{h}_{i}=\vec{h}_{i-1}\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{z}_{i}\odot_{\mathcal{L}}\left(-\vec{h}_{i-1}\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}\vec{\tilde{h}}_{i}\right)\,.

where the weight matrices Wh,r,zW_{h,r,z}, Uh,r,zU_{h,r,z} and bias vectors have the same meaning as previously defined. The various Lorentz mathematical operations appearing Eqs.(26), (27) are defined in terms of the exponential/logarithm mappings at 𝐱=𝟎ℒ\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}} in (22), (23) and parallel transport operations given in (25) as follows.

  • •

    For 𝐱,𝐲∈ℍn\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{H}^{n}, the Lorentz addition ⊕ℒ\oplus_{\mathcal{L}} is defined as:

    Lorentz addition:𝐱⊕ℒ𝐲=exp𝐱[P𝟎ℒ→𝐱(log𝟎ℒ(𝐲))]\displaystyle\text{Lorentz addition}:\qquad\mathbf{x}\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}\mathbf{y}=\exp_{\mathbf{x}}\left[P_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}\rightarrow\mathbf{x}}(\log_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}}(\mathbf{y}))\right] (28)
  • •

    The scalar multiplication ⊙ℒ\odot_{\mathcal{L}} between a point 𝐱∈ℍn\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{H}^{n} and r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R} is

    Lorentz scalar multiplication:r⊙ℒ𝐱=exp𝟎ℒ⁡[r​log𝟎ℒ⁡(𝐱)]\displaystyle\text{Lorentz scalar multiplication}:\qquad r\odot_{\mathcal{L}}\mathbf{x}=\exp_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}}\left[r\log_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}}(\mathbf{x})\right] (29)
  • •

    The matrix multiplication ⊗ℒ\otimes_{\mathcal{L}} between a point 𝐱∈ℍn\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{H}^{n} and a matrix M∈ℝn×ℝnM\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n} is

    M⊗ℒ𝐱=exp𝟎ℒ⁡[M​log𝟎ℒ⁡(𝐱)]\displaystyle M\otimes_{\mathcal{L}}\mathbf{x}=\exp_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}}\left[M\log_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}}(\mathbf{x})\right] (30)

In Eqs.(26), (27), the RNN/GRU hidden state h→i\vec{h}_{i} at the end of each computation is hyperbolic and lives on the Lorentz hyperboloid. The weight matrices Wh,r,z,Uh,r,zW_{h,r,z},U_{h,r,z} are Euclidean, while the biases b→h,r,z\vec{b}_{h,r,z} can be hyperbolic or Euclidean (in which case, they are projected onto the hyperboloid using the exponential map exp𝟎ℒ\exp_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}}). For the Lorentz GRU, the last equation in Eq.(27) is the update step for the hidden state h→i\vec{h}_{i}, which was done on the hyperboloid in an identical manner to the Poincaré case44 4 We note that it is also possible to define the update step using the tangent space as follows: h→i=h→i−1⊕ℒexp𝟎ℒ{z→i∗[log𝟎ℒ(h~→i)−log𝟎ℒ(h→i−1)]}\displaystyle\vec{h}_{i}=\vec{h}_{i-1}\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}\exp_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}}\left\{\vec{z}_{i}\,*\left[\log_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}}(\vec{\tilde{h}}_{i})-\log_{\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}}(\vec{h}_{i-1})\right]\right\} (31) where the hyperbolic hidden states h~→i\vec{\tilde{h}}_{i} and h→i−1\vec{h}_{i-1} have to be projected to the tangent space first before the subtraction is done, and the resulting state is multiplied with z→i\vec{z}_{i} in the tangent space before the exponential map that projects the result back on the hyperboloid, to be added to the hyperbolic state h→i−1\vec{h}_{i-1}. However, this definition relies heavily on the tangent space and is not as elegant as the one above, defined using the manifold primarily. . However, it must be noted that in Lorentz hyperbolic space, the state −h→i−1-\vec{h}_{i-1} is not simply the state h→i−1\vec{h}_{i-1} with all components multiplied by −1-1 (as is the case in Euclidean space as well as in the Poincaré disk). Instead, the −h→i−1-\vec{h}_{i-1} state has the components (x0,−x→i)(x_{0},-\vec{x}_{i}) if h→i−1=(x0,x→i)\vec{h}_{i-1}=(x_{0},\vec{x}_{i}), since we need h→i−1⊕ℒ(−h→i−1)=𝟎ℒ\vec{h}_{i-1}\oplus_{\mathcal{L}}(-\vec{h}_{i-1})=\mathbf{0}_{\mathcal{L}}.

3 Hyperbolic RNN-based NQS wavefunctions

In this section, we summarize the main points regarding the variational Monte-Carlo method, as well as the constructions of the real and complex NQS wavefunction using either Euclidean or hyperbolic RNN/GRU in discrete Hamiltonian spin systems. The detailed description can be found in [11], [22].

Variational Monte Carlo (VMC): The variational Monte Carlo (VMC) method, often used to train NQS, involves the process of sampling from a probability distribution represented by the square of the trial wavefunction/the variational ansatz and subsequently using these generated samples to calculate some obervables such as the ground state energy. In this section, we recall the derivation of the local energy formula in the Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) method [21].

Given a quantum Hamiltonian HH, in VMC, the local energy Eloc​(x)E_{\text{loc}}(x) of samples |x⟩|x\rangle generated by an NQS Ψ\Psi is given by

Eloc​(x)=∑x′⟨x|H|x′⟩​⟨x′|Ψ⟩⟨x|Ψ⟩.\displaystyle E_{\text{loc}}(x)=\sum_{x^{\prime}}\langle x|H|x^{\prime}\rangle\frac{\langle x^{\prime}|\Psi\rangle}{\langle x|\Psi\rangle}. (32)

Eloc​(x)E_{\text{loc}}(x) is non-zero only for those non-zero Hamiltonian elements ⟨x|H|x′⟩≠0\langle x|H|x^{\prime}\rangle\neq 0. Corresponding to each generated sample |x⟩|x\rangle is a probability

Ploc​(x)=|Ψ⁡(x)|2∑|x⟩|Ψ⁡(x)|2\displaystyle P_{\text{loc}}(x)=\frac{|\Psi(x)|^{2}}{\sum_{|x\rangle}|\Psi(x)|^{2}} (33)

In the variational problem of interest, given a Hamiltonian HH and a trial wavefunction Ψ\Psi, the VMC task is to estimate the ground state energy E=⟨Ψ|H|Ψ⟩E=\langle\Psi|H|\Psi\rangle which can be written in terms of the local energy ElocE_{\text{loc}} and the probability Ploc​(x)P_{\text{loc}}(x)

E=∑|x⟩Ploc​(x)​Eloc​(x).\displaystyle E=\sum_{|x\rangle}P_{\text{loc}}(x)E_{\text{loc}}(x)\,. (34)

When the trial wavefunction is a neural network quantum state |Ψ⁡(θ→)⟩|\Psi(\vec{\theta})\rangle with trainable parameters θ→\vec{\theta}, at each training iteration ii, the variational energy E⁡(θ→)E(\vec{\theta}) is calculated from the local energy Eloc​(θ→)E_{\text{loc}}(\vec{\theta}) of the Monte Carlo samples generated from the NQS using Eq.(34). The process of minimizing E⁡(θ→)E(\vec{\theta}) using an optimizer (such as SGD - Stochastic Gradient Descent or Adam - Adaptive Moment Estimation) updates the trainable parameters θ→\vec{\theta} until convergence is reached.

For the ensuing discussion below regarding the constructions of the real and complex NQS ansätze, the basis state of the Hamiltonian HH is denoted by |σ→⟩=(σ1,…,σN)|\vec{\sigma}\rangle=({\sigma}_{1},\ldots,{\sigma}_{N}) where NN is the dimensionality of HH, and each component σi​(1≤i≤N){\sigma}_{i}(1\leq i\leq N) assumes discrete values of either 0 or 1.

  • •

    Real NQS wavefunction: The wavefunction is defined as

    |Ψ⟩=∑σ→P⁡(σ→)​|σ→⟩\displaystyle|\Psi\rangle=\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}\sqrt{P(\vec{\sigma})}|\vec{\sigma}\rangle (35)

    where P⁡(σ→)P(\vec{\sigma}), the probability of a particular configuration |σ→⟩|\vec{\sigma}\rangle, is the output of the real NQS.

    P⁡(σ→)=P⁡(σ1)​P​(σ2|σ1)​…​P​(σN|σ1,σ2,…,σN−1)\displaystyle P(\vec{\sigma})=P({\sigma}_{1})P({\sigma}_{2}|{\sigma}_{1})\ldots P({\sigma}_{N}|{\sigma}_{1},{\sigma}_{2},\ldots,{\sigma}_{N-1}) (36)

    The autoregressive RNN-based real NQS wavefunction, whose schematic is shown in Fig.1, consists of a layer of RNN/GRU followed by a dense layer of 2 units with the Softmax activation function. The RNN/GRU layer can be Euclidean or hyperbolic, with the latter choice includes both the options of Poincaré and Lorentz models of hyperbolic space. The structure of the RNN-based real NQS function is illustrated in Fig.1. At a step ii where 0≤i≤N0\leq i\leq N, the RNN/GRU cell takes in two arguments, one being the previous RNN/GRU hidden state h→i−1\vec{h}_{i-1} and the input σ→i−1\vec{\sigma}_{i-1} (the one-hot-encoded (i−1)t​h(i-1)^{th} component of the generated spin sample σ→=(σ1,…,σN)\vec{\sigma}=({\sigma}_{1},\ldots,{\sigma}_{N})), to calculate the current RNN/GRU hidden state h→i\vec{h}_{i}. This is then passed into the Dense layer with the Softmax activation function55 5 Recall that the Softmax function is defined as Softmax​(vk)=exp⁡(vk)∑iexp⁡(vi)\displaystyle\text{Softmax}(v_{k})=\frac{\exp(v_{k})}{\sum_{i}\exp(v_{i})} (37) to obtain an output y→i\vec{y}_{i}, which is multiplied with the one-hot-encoded sample σi\sigma_{i} to calculate the probability P⁡(σ→i)P(\vec{\sigma}_{i}). The total probability P⁡(σ→)P(\vec{\sigma}) for the single spin sample σ→\vec{\sigma} is the product of all individual P⁡(σ→i)P(\vec{\sigma}_{i}).

  • •

    Complex NQS wavefunction : The complex NQS wavefunction is defined as

    Ψ⁡(σ→)=∑σ→exp⁡(i​ϕ​(σ→))​P⁡(σ→)​|σ→⟩.\displaystyle\Psi(\vec{\sigma})=\sum_{\vec{\sigma}}\exp(i\phi(\vec{\sigma}))\sqrt{P(\vec{\sigma})}|\vec{\sigma}\rangle\,. (38)

    where P⁡(σ→)P(\vec{\sigma}) has the same meaning as the real NQS case, while ϕ⁡(σ→)\phi(\vec{\sigma}) is the phase of the generated spin sample σ→\vec{\sigma}.

    The structure of the autoregressive RNN-based complex NQS wavefunction is illustrated in Fig.2 where SS and S​SSS represent the two Dense layers, one with Softmax activation and one with Softsign activation66 6 The Softsign function is defined as Softsign​(x)=x1+|x|∈(−1,1).\displaystyle\text{Softsign}(x)=\frac{x}{1+|x|}\in(-1,1)\,. (39) . Overall, this structure differs from that of the real RNN-based NQS shown in Fig.1 by the additional Softsign Dense layer that is used to generate the phase ϕ⁡(σ→)\phi(\vec{\sigma}). The computation of the real part P⁡(σ→)P(\vec{\sigma}) is the same as described in the real NQS case above, and will not be repeated here. To compute ϕ⁡(σ→)\phi(\vec{\sigma}), the hidden state h→i\vec{h}_{i} from the RNN/GRU cell is passed into the Softsign Dense layer to generated the output y→i(2)\vec{y}^{(2)}_{i}, which is then multiplied with σ→i\vec{\sigma}_{i} (the one-hot-encoded it​hi^{th} component of the spin sample σ→\vec{\sigma}) to obtain ϕi\phi_{i}. The final phase of the spin configuration σ→=(σ1,…,σN)\vec{\sigma}=({\sigma}_{1},\ldots,{\sigma}_{N}) is the sum of the individual ϕi\phi_{i} phases.

    In this paper, we only work with the complex NQS wavefunction, since the Hamiltonian systems of interest to us are the Heisenberg models. Besides the details described above, we note that the Marshall sign [42] was used in all experiments. As such, the wavefunction Ψ⁡(σ→)\Psi(\vec{\sigma}) is modified to be

    ΨM​(σ→)=(−1)MA​(σ→)​Ψ​(σ→)\displaystyle\Psi_{M}(\vec{\sigma})=(-1)^{M_{A}(\vec{\sigma})}\Psi(\vec{\sigma}) (40)

    where MA​(σ→)=∑k∈AσkM_{A}(\vec{\sigma})=\sum_{k\in A}{\sigma}_{k}, with AA containing the sites of either all even or all odd positions in the lattice. The factor (−1)MA​(σ→)(-1)^{M_{A}(\vec{\sigma})} is the Marshall sign of the wavefunction, while Ψ⁡(σ→)\Psi(\vec{\sigma}) is the complex wavefunction before the application of the Marshall sign. We note that Eq.(40) is exact only for the case of unfrustrated Heisenberg systems with only J1J_{1}, representing nearest neighbor interactions, nonvanishing (Ji≥1=0J_{i\geq 1}=0). In the case Ji≥1≠0J_{i\geq 1}\neq 0 where multiple degrees of nearest neighbor interactions are present, Eq.(40) only hold approximately.

Further remarks: Before moving on to the VMC experiments in the specific Heisenberg models, we note the following details that are common to all experiments done in this work.

  • •

    Due to our limited computing resources, we restricted the sizes of all neural networks to be relatively small, ranging on the orders of a few to tens of thousands parameters only, in order to carry out a large number of experiments. Our aim is not to use very large models to get a very high level of quantitative accuracy in the VMC energy (e.g. up to six digits) but to benchmark the qualitative performances of the hyperbolic RNN/GRU NQS ansätze with respect to the Euclidean RNN/GRU NQS ansätze, whose capability to attain a very high level of accuracy was already demonstrated in [11], [13].

  • •

    During the training phase, the number of spin configurations generated is fixed at 80 for all six types of NQS ansätze (Euclidean RNN, Poincaré RNN, Lorentz RNN, Euclidean GRU, Poincaré GRU, Lorentz GRU) used in this work. For inference, we used 10410^{4} spin configuration samples. As explained in [22], the choice of the relatively small number of 80 samples77 7 During the training process, we used two kinds of sampling: with and without the ‘temperature’ parameter τ\tau (set to 1.05 at the start of the training, decaying to 1 after 500 epochs) which encourages the model to stay in the exploration phase longer (before convergence). When τ≠1\tau\neq 1, the model is ‘encouraged’ to sample more diversely, while when τ=1.0\tau=1.0, the model defaults to its natural sampling state. For Poincaré GRU/RNN NQS as well as Euclidean RNN/GRU NQS, there were no noticeable differences in the obtained results with or without τ\tau, but for Lorentz RNN/GRU NQS, the trainings with τ\tau involved seemed to be marginally better than the ones without. Qualitatively this makes sense because Poincaré disk is a compact region while Lorentz hyperboloid is more open so in the latter case more explorations might lead to better optimizations while in the former case they might not. In the Euclidean case, qualitatively, the fact that τ\tau did not lead to a difference is probably due to the flat optimization landscape which does not benefit as much as the open hyperboloid landscape that is harder to navigate. For inference, τ\tau was not used in the sampling process (since the models had converged). (during training) was made based on the known fact that RNN-based, autoregressive NQS do not require too many samples to achieve convergence since an autoregressive architecture allows for an exact and independent sampling process by forward-generating spins from conditional distributions (with no Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling required). Furthermore, we used the practice of saving the best model during training, as explained in detail in [22], which means that the weights and biases of the model under training were saved only if the model showed improvement both in terms of a lower mean energy and a variance being under a specified variance tolerance threshold.

  • •

    For the Euclidean NQS ansätze, we used Adam optimizer with a scheduled learning rate decay contingent on the model reaching an energy plateau. For the Poincaré hyperbolic NQS ansätze, Adam optimizer was used for the Euclidean parameters (consisting of the weight matrices) and Riemannian SGD optimizer [38], [39] , [40] was used for the hyperbolic parameters (the biases). For the Lorentz hyperbolic NQS ansätze, both the weight matrices and the biases are Euclidean so Adam optimizer was used for all parameters. Similar to the Euclidean case, the same scheduled learning rate decay mechanism was applied to the Poincaré and Lorentz neural network training. We used the learning rate of 5×10−35\times 10^{-3} for the Euclidean parameters of all networks, while for the hyperbolic parameters (the biases), which are sensitive to the manifold geometry, the best learning rate had to be chosen via a process of trial and error to obtain the most stable training process. As such, the learning rate of the hyperbolic parameters can either be the same as the Euclidean parameters or different, depending on the problem at hand. For all our experiments, the hyperbolic learning rates are typically one of the following four choices: 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}, 1×10−31\times 10^{-3}, 5×10−35\times 10^{-3}, 8×10−38\times 10^{-3} and these are tested on each hyperbolic NQS to determine the one that yielded the best result. Furthermore, it must be noted that for the Lorentz networks, although the biases are Euclidean, they are transformed via the exponential map to be hyperbolic variables to be added on the manifold, so they can be subjected to a hyperbolic learning rate while the strictly Euclidean weight matrices are subjected to the Euclidean learning rate.

  • •

    As noted in [22], hyperbolic networks were expected to take much longer to train than Euclidean networks due to their much more complicated mathematical constructions involving manifold-native operations. While this is still the case for the experiments done in this work, the training durations of the Poincaré hyperbolic networks have been significantly improved by a factor of at least 5 times compared to our previous work, thanks to some optimizations carried out in the new Pytorch code which eliminated the redundancies present in the previous TensorFlow codes in the probability calculations of the NQS ansätze. In our previous work [22], we noted that Poincaré GRU could take more than 10 hours to train, but with the new code, the training time for Poincaré GRU is only around twice that of Euclidean GRU (around 2-3 hours). Poincaré RNN and Lorentz RNN are relatively fast to train, with the time taken being comparable to that taken by Euclidean GRU. Lorentz GRU, on the other hand, took much longer to train (up to more than 10 hours) than Poincaré GRU.

  • •

    Finally, for both Euclidean and hyperbolic networks, we used gradient clipping during the training process to ensure stable convergence. However, unlike the Euclidean RNN and GRU NQS ansätze which almost always delivered a stable behavior during training with just gradient clipping, due to the exponential growth of space in hyperbolic geometry, both Poincaré and Lorentz hyperbolic networks are naturally prone to additional numerical instabilities during the training process. Recall that Poincaré model is a bounded disk with an edge of radius c=1.0c=1.0, while Lorentz model is an open hyperboloid embedded in the Minkowski space with one extra spatial dimension. Instabilities in the form of ‘numerical explosions’ can occur in either model, with different underlying causes. For Poincaré RNN/GRU, unstable behaviors typically happen when the norm of the hidden state h→i\vec{h}_{i} is pushed to the edge of the Poincaré disk (at 1.0), reaching the value of 0.9999. For Lorentz RNN/GRU, unstable behaviors typically happened when the spatial (and time) components of the hidden state vector h→i\vec{h}_{i} grows exponentially large (like 102,10310^{2},10^{3}), causing the state to be pushed off the hyperboloid. When these numerical explosions happen, the hyperbolic models can drift around without settling into a minimum or even get trapped in a local mininum, causing the mean energy to stall at a value much higher than the true ground state. For this reason, to make sure that we obtained stable behaviors, a maximal radius Rm​a​x<cR_{max}<c was chosen for the Poincaré NQS, and a maximal spatial norm Lm​a​xL_{max} constraint on the spatial components of all hyperbolic vectors was implemented for the Lorentz models. These necessary measures ensured that the hidden state h→i\vec{h}_{i} of the hyperbolic RNN/GRU models was well-behaved, which translated into stable performances of the hyperbolic networks during the training process. The maximal radius Rm​a​xR_{max} in Poincaré disk and the maximal spatial norm clamp Lm​a​xL_{max} in Lorentz hyperboloid are therefore additional hyperparameters for the hyperbolic networks that must be chosen carefully to obtain optimal performances of these networks. More details on these hyperparameters for each specific Heisenberg model will be discussed in the sections below, as well as in the Appendix, Section 7.1.

4 1D Heiseinberg J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} Model

The first Hamiltonian system of interest to us is the frustrated 1D Heisenberg J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model

HJ​1​J​2=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩Si​Sj+J2​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩Si​Sj,\displaystyle H_{J1J2}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}S_{i}S_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle}S_{i}S_{j}, (41)

with open boundary condition, where SiS_{i} denoting the Pauli spin half operators. The Hamiltonian is a sum of two terms: the first takes into account the nearest neighbor interactions pairs ⟨i,j⟩\langle i,j\rangle, the second takes into account the next nearest neighbor interaction pairs ⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle. In this work, we are interested in the case of antiferromagnetic couplings where both J1>0J_{1}>0 and J2>0J_{2}>0. The physics of the 1D J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model at different couplings J2J_{2} is well studied [41] and is very briefly summarized below.

  • •

    At J2=0.0J_{2}=0.0, the system exists in a gapless Luttinger liquid phase with translation symmetry.

  • •

    At J2=0.2J_{2}=0.2, the system still exists in the Luttinger liquid phase, albeit with frustration, with translation symmetry intact. At J2=0.2412J_{2}=0.2412, the system exhibits a phase transition from a critical Luttinger liquid phase to a spontaneously gapped valence phase, more generally known as the ‘dimer’ phase where adjacent spins form pairs and translation symmetry is broken.

  • •

    At J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5, the second neighbor coupling is exactly half as strong as the first neighbor coupling J1J_{1}, the model reduces to the Majumdar-Ghosh model where the quantum system is exactly solvable and the ground state is a perfectly commensurate dimer phase (where the spins alternate exactly on every other site).

  • •

    At J2=0.8J_{2}=0.8, the system is highly frustrated as J2J_{2} is almost as large as J1J_{1}, and the ground state is generally known to exist in an incommensurate dimer phase (where a spiral pattern exists alongside the spin alignment).

To study the performances of Poincaré and Lorentz hyperbolic RNN/GRU NQS ansätze versus the Euclidean RNN/GRU NQS ansätze, we fixed the number of spins in the system to be N=100N=100 (exactly two times larger than the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} system studied in [22]), the coupling J1=1.0J_{1}=1.0 and varied J2=0.0,0.2,0.5,0.8J_{2}=0.0,0.2,0.5,0.8 in the same fashion as in our earlier work [22]. The exact energy of the four Heisenberg models were calculated with DMRG (Density Matrix Renormalization Group) method.

We list the six types of NQS wavefunctions that were used to run VMC experiments for this system in Table 1. As already noted in [22], the aim of our work is to establish the performances of the new hyperbolic RNN/GRU NQS ansätze relative to the well-established Euclidean RNN/GRU NQS ansätze ([11], [13]), so the inclusion of the Euclidean RNN/GRU NQS ansätze in our experiments served purely as benchmarks for the new hyperbolic NQS. For the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} experiment settings, all RNN/GRU had the same h→i\vec{h}_{i} hidden dimension size of 70 units, meaning that the RNN variants had 2.895 times fewer parameters than the GRU variants (where each GRU/RNN variant contains three different types of neural networks: Euclidean, Poincaré and Lorentz). This choice was motivated by the fact that in designing our experiments, the size of the hidden dimension h→\vec{h} of the RNN/GRU mattered to us more than the total number of parameters. The results listed in Table 2 correspond to the best achievable results for each of the six NQS ansätze chosen from multiple VMC runs while those listed in Table 3 correspond to the averaged results for each NQS ansatz taken from all VMC runs, where a single VMC run is defined by a distinct random seed, where each seed corresponds to a different initialization configuration before training starts. The full results corresponding to all individual random seeds are listed in Section 7.2.1 for all six types of NQS.

For this set of experiments, we fixed the number of training epochs to 1000, with an early stopping mechanism built in to terminate the training early in case no improvement was registered for a period of 200 epochs. As such, the number of training epochs varied for each NQS. As mentioned above, we used a variable learning rate scheme ReduceLROnPlateau which automatically decays the learning rate (for both Euclidean and hyperbolic parameters) by a factor of 2.0 when no improvements are detected within 40 epochs88 8 Besides the main difference being Pytorch rather than TensorFlow in this work compared to [22], the use of ReduceLROnPlateau differed from the learning rate decay mechanism used in [22] in which the learning rate of Euclidean parameters was subjected to a decay factor of 0.9 every 100 epochs while the hyperbolic learning rate was kept fixed, with both initial learning rates set to be 10−210^{-2}.. The initial learning rate for Euclidean parameters of both Euclidean and hyperbolic networks was fixed at 5×10−35\times 10^{-3}, while the initial learning rate for hyperbolic parameters was chosen on a case-by-case and trial-and-error basis. Most often, the initial hyperbolic learning rate was fixed at either 5×10−35\times 10^{-3} (same as Euclidean parameters) or 8×10−38\times 10^{-3}.

Also as mentioned previously, Euclidean NQS were straightforward to train and they almost always delivered stable performances, largely thanks to the fact that besides choosing the number of RNN/GRU hidden dimensions and the initial learning rate for the Euclidean parameters, there is no other hyperparameter that required special attention. On the other hand, hyperbolic networks have more hyperparameters in the form of the hyperbolic learning rate as well as an additional hyperparameter - the maximal radius Rm​a​xR_{max} for the Poincaré networks or the maximal spatial norm Lm​a​xL_{max} for the Lorentz networks, which we will collectively refer to as the spatial constraint hyperparameter - that must be chosen very carefully to ensure the best performances that hyperbolic network can deliver. Unsuitable choices of this spatial constraint hyperparameter lead to poor and unstable performances by hyperbolic networks (see the discussion in Section 7.1 in the Appendix). The specific choices (obtained through a rather laborious and tedious process of trial-and-error) of Rm​a​xR_{max} and Lm​a​xL_{max} for the hyperbolic networks are listed in Table 9 and 11, respectively (Section 7.1).

From Table 2 and Table 3, as well as Figs. 3, 4, the following observations are made.

  • •

    Architecture-wise, in terms of the best achievable mean energy (see Table 2), within an architecture variant (either RNN or GRU), for all J2J_{2} values, hyperbolic NQS ansätze always outperformed their Euclidean counterparts, i.e. Poincaré RNN and Lorentz RNN always outperformed Euclidean RNN, and Poincaré GRU and Lorentz GRU always outperformed Euclidean GRU. This is the generalization of the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} results reported in [22] in which we only constructed and introduced a single form of NQS hyperbolic network - the Poincaré hyperbolic GRU, which was benchmarked agains the Euclidean GRU for J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} Heisenberg system with 50 spins. More specifically, if we look at each architecture separately:

    1. 1.

      NQS ansätze with RNN architecture: Among the three RNN variants (with 5394 parameters), for all J2J_{2} couplings, Lorentz RNN is always the best performing NQS, followed by Poincaré RNN and Euclidean RNN. In particular, Euclidean RNN very often settles into a local minimum that is much higher than the true ground state and lags far behind both Poincaré and Lorentz RNN in terms of performance. Between the two hyperbolic RNNs, Poincaré RNN never even attains the level of performance comparable to Lorentz RNN, despite the supposed one-to-one mapping between Poincaré RNN and Lorentz RNN. At the moment, it is not clear to us whether this underperformance by Poincaré RNN can be more attributable to the lack of a comprehensive Rm​a​xR_{max} tuning or more to the inherent nature of the Poincaré RNN’s construction in the Poincaré disk.

    2. 2.

      NQS ansätze with GRU architecture: Among the three GRU variants (with 15614 parameters), depending on the specific J2J_{2} value, either Lorentz GRU or Poincaré GRU is the best performing NQS. In particular, at J2=0.0,0.5J_{2}=0.0,0.5, Lorentz GRU is the best performing variant, while for J2=0.2,0.8J_{2}=0.2,0.8, Poincaré GRU ranks first. Euclidean GRU always ranks third among the three GRU variants. The gaps between the performances of Euclidean GRU and its hyperbolic counterparts are very small, unlike the gaps between Euclidean RNN and its hyperbolic versions. For all J2J_{2} couplings, while Lorentz RNN clearly outperformed Poincaré RNN, the opposite is true for Poincaré GRU and Lorentz GRU, with each occupying the top spot two out of four times, making it an even split between Lorentz GRU and Poincaré GRU for the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} system.

  • •

    Across architectures: When all six NQS ansätze are compared, as shown in Figs.3 in terms of the best achievable mean energy, a very interesting picture emerged. While Euclidean RNN is consistently the worst performing variant, with Poincaré RNN consistently the second worst, the top four spots are held by Euclidean GRU, Poincaré GRU, Lorentz GRU and Lorentz RNN, in different orders depending on the specific value of J2J_{2}.

    • –

      J2=0.0J_{2}=0.0: Lorentz RNN is the top performer, with Lorentz GRU coming in second, followed by Poincaré GRU (third) and Euclidean GRU (fourth).

    • –

      J2=0.2J_{2}=0.2: Lorentz RNN again ranks first, followed by Poincaré GRU (second), Lorentz GRU (third), and Euclidean GRU (fourth).

    • –

      J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5: Lorentz GRU is the top performer, followed by Poincaré GRU (second), Euclidean GRU (third), Lorentz RNN (fourth).

    • –

      J2=0.8J_{2}=0.8: Poincaré GRU is the top performer, followed by Lorentz GRU (second), Euclidean GRU (third), Lorentz RNN (fourth).

    Among the four hyperbolic NQS ansätze, Poincaré RNN seems to be the least performant variant, as it underperformed Euclidean GRU, Lorentz RNN, Poincaré GRU and Lorentz GRU in all four experiments. While it was expected that the hyperbolic GRU ansätze would outperform Poincaré RNN and Lorentz RNN thanks to their sophisticated GRU gating mechanism and three times more parameters, Lorentz RNN defied expectations to deliver a surprising overall performance. On two occasions when J2=0.0,0.2J_{2}=0.0,0.2, Lorentz RNN was able to surpass all GRU variants to be the top performer, despite having almost three times fewer parameters. This might point to the possibility that for the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model at these low J2J_{2} couplings (corresponding to a low level of frustration in the system), the simpler hyperbolic RNN architecture is superior (in providing a ground state approximation to the Heisenberg model) to the more complex GRU gating mechanism, both in Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces. For J2=0.5,0.8J_{2}=0.5,0.8 where hyperbolic GRU variants (Poincaré and Lorentz) ranked in top two, Lorentz RNN underperformed all GRU variants including Euclidean GRU. This might be indicative of the possibility that for these highly frustrated cases where the ground state is in a dimerized phase, the pure hyperbolic geometry offered by Lorentz RNN was insufficient to surpass the sophisticated gating mechanism offered by Euclidean GRU and the combination of hyperbolic geometry and GRU gating mechanism embodied in both the Poincaré and Lorentz GRU.

    When the performances are ranked in terms of the averaged mean energy for each NQS ansatz obtained from all the VMC runs taken together, as shown in Fig.4, the emerging picture is slightly different but the major qualitative features similar to the ‘best achievable’ case above remain. In particular, Euclidean RNN is still the worst performing variant for all J2J_{2} values, with the rest of the NQS ranking in descending order as follows.

    • –

      J2=0.0J_{2}=0.0: Lorentz GRU is the top performer, with Poincaré GRU in the second spot, followed by Lorentz RNN (third) Euclidean GRU (fourth) and Poincaré RNN (fifth).

    • –

      J2=0.2J_{2}=0.2: Lorentz RNN ranks first, followed by Poincaré GRU (second), Lorentz GRU (third), and Euclidean GRU (fourth) and Poincaré RNN (fifth). This is the same as the ‘best achievable’ case above.

    • –

      J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5: Poincaré GRU ranks first, followed by Lorentz GRU (second), Lorentz RNN (third), Poincaré RNN (fourth) and Euclidean GRU (fifth). This is the only time when Poincaré RNN ranks above Euclidean GRU in the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} experiments.

    • –

      J2=0.8J_{2}=0.8: Poincaré GRU ranks first, followed by Lorentz GRU (second), Euclidean GRU (third), Lorentz RNN (fourth) and Poincaré RNN (fifth).

    From multiple VMC runs (see the full results for all NQS ansätze with different random seeds listed in Section 7.2.1 in the Appendix), we notice that for some of the random seeds, Poincaré RNN (see Table 15) and Lorentz RNN/GRU (Tables 17 and 18) failed to converge (i.e. the mean energy either settled into an artificially high value far away from the true ground state, e.g. like in the positive value range, or some sort of kinks or steps occurring in the training). Out of the four hyperbolic NQS, Poincaré GRU showed the most stable performance with no non-convergence issues (see Table 16), with obtained energy values differing little across different seeds. Poincaré RNN was most stable when J2=0.0,0.2J_{2}=0.0,0.2 with non-convergence issues for some of the seeds surfacing when J2=0.5,0.8J_{2}=0.5,0.8. Lorentz RNN was most stable when J2=0.2,0.5J_{2}=0.2,0.5 with less stability shown when J2=0.0,0.8J_{2}=0.0,0.8. Lorentz GRU was most stable when J2=0.0,0.2J_{2}=0.0,0.2 and less stable when J2=0.5,0.8J_{2}=0.5,0.8. However, the values obtained by all hyperbolic NQS when they did converge were consistently within a narrow range of one another without significant deviations. The instability of the hyperbolic NQS training is directly attributable to the fact that the Poincaré and Lorentz hyperbolic optimization landscapes, with their negative curvatures determined by the spatial constraints hyperparameters Rm​a​xR_{max} or Lm​a​xL_{max}, are much more ‘’rugged’ compared to the flat Euclidean optimization landscape. This is a challenge well known and well documented from NLP works dealing with hyperbolic neural networks [8], [27], [29], [31].

    While the challenge associated with hyperbolic optimization leads to the expectations that Euclidean variants should be much more stable in their trainings compared to their hyperbolic counterparts, interestingly, in our experiments, even the Euclidean variants showed wild fluctuations in terms of the obtained mean energies across different runs for some values of J2J_{2}. For example, at J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5 (where the energy is -37.5) at the Majumdar-Ghosh point, both Euclidean RNN NQS and Euclidean GRU NQS (see Tables 13 and 14) obtained inconsistent results. In four of five runs, Euclidean RNN NQS converged at the false minimum of around −12-12 to −13-13, with single run where it could achieve a much closer value of −35.06-35.06, which was its best achievable energy recorded in Table 2. In two out of five runs, Euclidean GRU NQS converged at the false minimum of around -36 and -30, while on the other three runs, it could reach below -37. In another example, when J2=0.8J_{2}=0.8 with E=−42.07E=-42.07, Euclidean RNN NQS converged at values ranging from −5.99-5.99 to −24.56-24.56. These observations highlight the fact that even for the stable and established Euclidean RNN/GRU NQS, statistical fluctuations in convergence characteristics do occur across multiple random seeds, so the training behaviors of the hyperbolic NQS observed in this work are within normal expectations, given the more challenging nature of the hyperbolic optimization process.

5 1D Heiseinberg J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} Model

The second Hamiltonian system of interest to us is the frustrated 1D Heisenberg J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model

HJ​1​J​2​J​3=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩Si​Sj+J2​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩Si​Sj+J3​∑⟨⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩⟩Si​Sj,\displaystyle H_{J1J2J3}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}S_{i}S_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle}S_{i}S_{j}+J_{3}\sum_{\langle\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle\rangle}S_{i}S_{j}, (42)

with open boundary condition, where SiS_{i} denoting the Pauli spin half operators. The Hamiltonian is a sum of three terms: the first takes into account the nearest neighbor interactions pairs ⟨i,j⟩\langle i,j\rangle, the second takes into account the second nearest neighbor interaction pairs ⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle, and the third takes into account the third nearest neighbor interactions. In this work, we are interested in the J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model with all antiferromagnetic couplings, i.e. Jn>0J_{n}>0 for n=1,2,3n=1,2,3, which means that the system is highly frustrated. The physics of the 1D J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model is much less studied than that of the 1D J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model in the literature. Perhaps the most recent work99 9 Two dimensional J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} models are more often studied than one-dimensional J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} models. on the 1D J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model is [45], in which the authors studied the J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model with a ferromagnetic coupling J1J_{1} and two antiferromagnetic couplings J2,J3J_{2},J_{3} to study the phase transition of the system.

In this work, our interest lies in approximating the ground states of the J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} Heisenberg models using the new hyperbolic NQS ansätze. Similar to the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} case above, and in the same manner to what was studied in our earlier work [22], we fixed J1=1.0J_{1}=1.0 and varied the couplings (J2CLOSE(J_{2}, OPENJ3)=(0.0,0.5)J_{3})=(0.0,0.5), (0.2,0.2), (0.2, 0.5) and (0.5, 0.2) to obtain different physical regimes under which the different NQS wavefunctions are used to approximate the true ground state energies. In this work, however, the number of spins is fixed to be N=100N=100 (more than three times larger than the case studied in [22]). While the exact physics of the 1D J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} in these coupling regimes requires more detailed studies which are beyond the scope of this work whose main aims are to establish the new types of hyperbolic RNN-based NQS ansätze, our choices of the (J2,J3)(J_{2},J_{3}) couplings here and in [22] were made with the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model in mind, namely we added either J3=0.2J_{3}=0.2 or J3=0.5J_{3}=0.5 to the previously chosen values of J2=0.0,0.2,0.5J_{2}=0.0,0.2,0.5 in the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model.

  • •

    When J3=0.2J_{3}=0.2, J3≤J2J_{3}\leq J_{2} as in (0.2,0.2) and (0.5,0.2): it can be assumed that the physics of the J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} models are reasonably close to that of the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model, based on the fact that the ground state energies are these two Heisenberg models are not too far apart, i.e. EJ2=0.5=−37.5000E_{J_{2}=0.5}=-37.5000 while E(0.5,0.2)=−38.54733E_{(0.5,0.2)}=-38.54733, E(0.2,0.2)=−43.5860E_{(0.2,0.2)}=-43.5860, while EJ2=0.2=−40.7388E_{J_{2}=0.2}=-40.7388.

  • •

    When J3=0.5J_{3}=0.5, J3>J2J_{3}>J_{2} as in (0.0,0.5), (0.2,0.5): the third neighbor interaction is dominant, and the physics of the two models are very different, with their corresponding ground state energies being very far apart, i.e. EJ2=0.0=−44.1277E_{J_{2}=0.0}=-44.1277, while E(0.0,0.5)=−53.9914E_{(0.0,0.5)}=-53.9914, EJ2=0.2=−40.7388E_{J_{2}=0.2}=-40.7388, while E(0.2,0.5)=−49.6287E_{(0.2,0.5)}=-49.6287.

We list in Table 4 the six types of RNN/GRU-based NQS ansätze that are used for this system. For the J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} experiment settings, all RNN variants had 80 units in the hidden dimension h→i\vec{h}_{i}, while the GRU variants had 70 units, meaning that the former had 2.242 times fewer parameters than the latter. All the details regarding the training of these NQS as well as the choices of the hyperparameters are identical to the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} case (except for the fact that the number of epochs were fixed to 1200 this time) and will not be repeated here. In Table 5, we list the best achievable results for each of the six NQS ansätze chosen from multiple VMC runs while in Table 6, we list the averaged results for each NQS ansatz taken from all VMC runs. The full results corresponding to all individual random seeds are listed in Section 7.2.2 for all six types of NQS. The choices of the spatial constraint hyperparameters Rm​a​xR_{max} and Lm​a​xL_{max} for the Poincaré and Lorentz hyperbolic neural networks are included in Table 10 and Table 12 in the Appendix.

From Table 5 and Table 6, as well as Figs.5, 6, we can make the following observations regarding the performance ranking of each NQS. Many details are identical to the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} case studied in the previous section, but there are also some important differences especially when it comes down to comparing the hyperbolic NQS ansätze corresponding to different hyperbolic sub-geometries.

  • •

    Architecture-wise, within the same architecture variant (either RNN or GRU), in terms of the best achievable mean energy (see Table 5 and Fig.5), hyperbolic NQS (either Lorentz or Poincaré) always outperformed Euclidean NQS. This result is the generalization of the J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} results reported in [22] where we established that Poincaré GRU almost always outperformed Euclidean GRU for J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} systems with 30 spins. In this more general results, with a larger physical system of 100 spins, we broadened the class of hyperbolic NQS to include not only Poincaré GRU but also Lorentz GRU as well as Poincaré and Lorentz RNN. More specifically, if we look at each architecture separately:

    1. 1.

      NQS ansätze with RNN architecture: Among the RNN variants with 6964 parameters, for all values of (J2,J3CLOSE(J_{2},J_{3}) couplings, Lorentz RNN is always the top performer, followed by Poincaré RNN. Euclidean RNN trailed them both by a very large margin. This is identical to what was observed in the 1D J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} case.

    2. 2.

      NQS ansätze with GRU architecture: Among the GRU variants with 15614 parameters, on three out of four occasions corresponding to the cases of (J2,J3)=(0.0,0.5)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.0,0.5), (0.2,0.2), (0.2,0.5), Lorentz GRU is the top performer, followed by Poincaré GRU. For the last case of (J2,J3)=(0.5,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.5,0.2), Poincaré outperformed Lorentz GRU. In all four cases, Euclidean GRU was outperformed by its two hyperbolic versions, which is the same as what was observed in the 1D J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} case. The difference in this case, compared to the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} case above, is the fact that it is no longer an even split between Lorentz GRU and Poincaré GRU but it is Lorentz GRU that outperformed Poincaré GRU three out of four times.

  • •

    Across architectures: When all six NQS ansätze are compared (see Fig.5) in terms of the best achievable mean energy that each ansatz could reach, the emerging picture in ascending performance order is as follows.

    1. 1.

      (J2,J3)=(0.0,0.5)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.0,0.5): Euclidean RNN (sixth), Poincaré RNN (fifth), Euclidean GRU (fourth), Poincaré GRU (third), Lorentz GRU (second), Lorentz RNN (first).

    2. 2.

      (J2,J3)=(0.2,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.2,0.2): Exact same order as (J2,J3)=(0.0,0.5)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.0,0.5).

    3. 3.

      (J2,J3)=(0.2,0.5)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.2,0.5): Exact same order as (J2,J3)=(0.0,0.5)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.0,0.5) and (J2,J3)=(0.2,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.2,0.2).

    4. 4.

      (J2,J3)=(0.5,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.5,0.2): Euclidean RNN (sixth), Poincaré RNN (fifth), Euclidean GRU (fourth), Lorentz GRU (third), Poincaré GRU (second), Lorentz RNN (first).

    Among the four hyperbolic NQS ansätze with different architectures, conforming to expectations, Poincaré GRU and Lorentz GRU outperformed Poincaré RNN in all four experiments due to the two former having the more complex GRU gating mechanism and nearly 2.25 times more parameters than the latter (15614 versus 6964). Again defying expections for all values of (J2,J3)(J_{2},J_{3}) couplings, Lorentz RNN showed a remarkable performance against all GRU variants, despite having around 2.25 times fewer parameters. It consistently ranked first placing ahead of all GRU variants including Euclidean GRU, Poincaré GRU and Lorentz GRU all four out of four times. Similar to the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} case, this result again demonstrates the possibility that the pure hyperbolic geometry underlying the Lorentz RNN can definitively deliver a more suitable representation of the ground state wavefunction than any GRU variant could. On the other hand, we cannot be sure that the surprising underperformance of Lorentz and Poincaré GRU in these experiments compared to Lorentz RNN is an actual fact or an artefact of their spatial constraint hyperparameter not being optimally selected.

    In terms of the averaged performance of each NQS ansatz obtained from taking the average of all VMC runs (see Fig.6), the emerging picture in ascending order is as follows.

    1. 1.

      (J2,J3)=(0.0,0.5)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.0,0.5): Euclidean RNN (sixth), Euclidean GRU (fifth), Poincaré RNN (fourth), Lorentz GRU (third), Poincaré GRU (second), Lorentz RNN (first).

    2. 2.

      (J2,J3)=(0.2,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.2,0.2): Euclidean RNN (sixth), Euclidean GRU (fifth), Poincaré RNN (fourth), Poincaré GRU (third), Lorentz GRU (second), Lorentz RNN (first).

    3. 3.

      (J2,J3)=(0.2,0.5)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.2,0.5): Euclidean RNN (sixth), Poincaré RNN (fifth), Lorentz GRU (fourth), Poincaré GRU (third), Euclidean GRU (second), Lorentz RNN (first).

    4. 4.

      (J2,J3)=(0.5,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.5,0.2): Euclidean RNN (sixth), Poincaré RNN (fifth), Poincaré GRU (fourth), Euclidean GRU (third), Lorentz GRU (second), Lorentz RNN (first).

    As in the case of J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model above, the difficulties and instability in training hyperbolic NQS ansätze persisted in this case as well. In particular, Lorentz GRU and RNN NQS failed to converge for all values of J2J_{2} with some of the random seeds (see Tables 23 and 24). When they did converge, the values actually stayed in a narrow range without significant deviations. As explained in detail in the previous J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} case, this behavior is expected since the hyperbolic optimization landscape is much harder to navigate compared to a flat, Euclidean one consisting only of flat directions. Interestingly, despite this hyperbolic optimization challenge, both Poincaré GRU and RNN NQS (see Tables 21 and 22) showed much more stability than the Lorentzian hyperbolic counterparts with only a single instance of non-convergence when (J2,J3)=(0.5,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.5,0.2) in all J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} experiments. Furthermore, Poincaré RNN/GRU also yielded very consistent mean energy values across mulitple random seeds.

    Conversely, for Euclidean GRU/RNN NQS ansätze (see Tables 19 and 20) which are supposedly more stable to train, we did run into the issues of inconsistent performances across different random seeds. One example of this occurred in the J2=0.0,J3=0.5J_{2}=0.0,J_{3}=0.5 case with Euclidean GRU NQS, which yielded a mean energy in the range [-37, -38] for three of five seeds, with one seed failing to converge and the last seed performing particularly well and obtaining -53.29. Another example also involves Euclidean GRU failing to converge on one instance when (J2,J3)=(0.5,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.5,0.2). Stability-wise, we observe that while Euclidean GRU NQS failed to converge on two instances, Poincaré GRU and RNN NQS only failed to converge on one occasion, meaning that the Poincaré hyperbolic variants were actually more stable in training than the Euclidean GRU NQS in this set of J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} experiments.

    Furthermore, when the averaged results are taken into account, it is interesting to see that Poincaré RNN did outperform Euclidean GRU on two occasions when (J2,J3)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.0, 0.5), (0.2, 0.2). Lorentz RNN, in particular, still ranked first despite its inherent instability in the training process across different seeds because when it did converge, the values are actually very consistently close to the true ground state energy with only minor fluctuations.

6 Summary and future directions

In this work, we constructed novel types of hyperbolic NQS ansätze based on the additional types of hyperbolic RNNs including Poincaré RNN, Lorentz RNN, and Lorentz GRU, alongside the Poincaré GRU NQS which was first constructed in our previous work [22]. On the one hand, the formulations of the Lorentz RNN/GRU as standalone Lorentz recurrent architectures are the first constructions of their kinds and constitute one of the main novelties of this work. On the other hand, in introducing these new types of hyperbolic NQS ansätze and extending the experiments of [22] to the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} and J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} Heisenberg models with 100 spins (twice the number of spins considered for the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model in [22] and three times the system size considered for J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} in [22]), we not only reproduced and confirmed the results of [22] showing that Poincaré GRU always outperforming Euclidean GRU for all the J2J_{2} and (J2,J3)(J_{2},J_{3}) couplings studied, but also generalized these results to include the three new types of hyperbolic NQS introduced here.

Given the different varieties of the six NQS ansätze studied in this work, which span two geometries (Euclidean versus hyperbolic) including two hyperbolic sub-geometries (Poincaré disk versus Lorentz hyperboloid) and two different neural network architectures (RNN versus GRU), different kinds of performance comparisons can be made based on either the criterion of geometry, architecture or both. In what follows, we will use the results of our VMC experiments - collectively, across the eight different experiment settings corresponding to Heisenberg J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} model with J2=0.0J_{2}=0.0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8 and Heisenberg J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} model with (J2,J3J_{2},J_{3})=(0.0, 0.5), (0.2,0.2), (0.2, 0.5), (0.5, 0.2) - to make the comparisons based on all possible combinations of criteria, in tems of both the best obtained and averaged results from multiple VMC runs using different random seeds. Since the ‘best achievable’ result of each NQS ansatz (chosen from different VMC runs) represents its absolute capacity while the averaged results represent the stability of the ansatz, we will focus more on the former to make the comparisons, as we are ultimately interested in the best values reachable by each ansatz. To facilitate the comparisons, we listed in Table 7 and Table 8 the top three best performing NQS ansätze (in terms of best achievable mean energy) for each of the eight experiments1010 10 where one experiment corresponding to either a single value of J2J_{2} or the pair (J2,J3)(J_{2},J_{3}) consists of at least 30 different VMC runs where each of the 6 NQS ansätze was used with 5 different random seeds. This is not inclusive of the many more VMC runs required to tune the various hyperparameters of the hyperbolic Poincaré and Lorentz NQS in order to select the optimal spatial constraint parameters Rm​a​xR_{max} and Lm​a​xL_{max}.

  1. 1.

    Between hyperbolic and Euclidean NQS ansätze of the same architecture (in other words, comparing Euclidean versus hyperbolic geometry):

    1. i.

      Poincaré RNN and Lorentz RNN, the newly introduced hyperbolic RNN NQS ansätze in this work, always outperformed Euclidean RNN in all experiments (including J2=0.0J_{2}=0.0).

    2. ii.

      Lorentz GRU - the newly introduced hyperbolic GRU NQS ansatz in this work, and Poincaré GRU - the previously introduced hyperbolic GRU NQS ansatz from [22], always outperformed Euclidean GRU, in all experiments (including J2=0.0J_{2}=0.0).

    These observations point towards the fact that within the same neural network architecture (where the NQS ansätze have the same number of parameters), the Poincaré and Lorentz hyperbolic variants (either RNN or GRU) might be potentially superior to and very likely outperform the corresponding Euclidean variant (either RNN or GRU) in this problem of approximating the ground state wavefunction of Heisenberg spin systems with varying hierarchical degrees of nearest neighbor couplings. With these, the primary goal of this work, which concerns the generalizations of our previous results reported in [22], which only included two NQS ansätze - the Euclidean and Poincaré GRU - in the J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} and J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} models, to all four hyperbolic NQS variants, is achieved.

  2. 2.

    Between hyperbolic NQS ansätze of the same architecture (in other words, comparing the hyperbolic sub-geometry of Poincaré model versus Lorentz model):

    1. i.

      RNN architecture: The Lorentz hyperboloid geometry wins here, with Lorentz RNN definitively outperformed Poincaré RNN, for all couplings considered in all experiments.

    2. ii.

      GRU architecture: Poincaré GRU outperformed Lorentz GRU three out of eight times - twice in J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} experiments (OPENJ2=0.2,0.8)J_{2}=0.2,0.8), and once in J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} experiments when (J2,J3)=(0.5,0.2)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.5,0.2). Conversely, Lorentz GRU outperformed Poincaré GRU five out of eight times, twice in J1​J2J_{1}J_{2} experiments when J2=0.0,0.5J_{2}=0.0,0.5, and thrice in J1​J2​J3J_{1}J_{2}J_{3} experiments when (J2,J3)=(0.0,0.5)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.0,0.5), (0.2,0.2), (0.2,0.5).

    These observations point towards the likelihood that the Lorentz model of hyperbolic space is potentially superior to the Poincaré model, given the number of times the Lorentz variant collectively outperformed the Poincaré variant across two different architectures.
